claim: The mammalian suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) drives daily rhythmic behavior and physiology.
source: The mammalian suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) drives daily rhythmic behavior and physiology, yet a detailed understanding of its coordinated transcriptional programmes is lacking.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in circadian biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: 7-times more genes exhibited a classic sinusoidal expression signature than previously observed in the SCN.
source: We show that 7-times more genes exhibited a classic sinusoidal expression signature than previously observed in the SCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis comparing the current study to previous microarray studies.

claim: 766 genes unexpectedly peaked twice, near both the start and end of the dark phase.
source: Another group of 766 genes unexpectedly peaked twice, near both the start and end of the dark phase
evidence: This is supported by WGCNA analysis of the RNA-seq data identifying the twin-peaking module.

claim: The twin-peaking group is significantly enriched for synaptic transmission genes that are crucial for light-induced phase shifting of the circadian clock.
source: this twin-peaking group is significantly enriched for synaptic transmission genes that are crucial for light-induced phase shifting of the circadian clock.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis of the twin-peaking genes and their known roles in phase shifting.

claim: 341 intergenic non-coding RNAs show specific circadian expression variation.
source: 341 intergenic non-coding RNAs, together with novel exons of annotated protein-coding genes, including Cry1, also show specific circadian expression variation.
evidence: This is supported by the identification and temporal analysis of lincRNAs from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Novel exons of annotated protein-coding genes, including Cry1, show specific circadian expression variation.
source: 341 intergenic non-coding RNAs, together with novel exons of annotated protein-coding genes, including Cry1, also show specific circadian expression variation.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of novel exons and their temporal expression patterns in the RNA-seq data.

claim: Transcriptional timing in the SCN is gating clock resetting mechanisms.
source: Overall, our data provide an important chronobiological resource (www.wgpembroke.com/shiny/SCNseq/) and allow us to propose that transcriptional timing in the SCN is gating clock resetting mechanisms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between twin-peaking gene expression and phase response curve susceptibility windows.

claim: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the seat of the principal circadian clock in mammals.
source: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the seat of the principal circadian clock in mammals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in chronobiology.

claim: The SCN is entrained by photic information and other external stimuli.
source: Entrained by photic information and other external stimuli, this group of neurons maintains 24-hr rhythms of physiology and behaviour by synchronising molecular oscillators in the brain and peripheral tissues (Welsh et al., 2010; Ko and Takahashi, 2006; Maywood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The SCN maintains 24-hr rhythms of physiology and behaviour by synchronising molecular oscillators in the brain and peripheral tissues.
source: Entrained by photic information and other external stimuli, this group of neurons maintains 24-hr rhythms of physiology and behaviour by synchronising molecular oscillators in the brain and peripheral tissues (Welsh et al., 2010; Ko and Takahashi, 2006; Maywood et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The transcriptional output of the SCN is critical for biological adaptation to night and day.
source: The transcriptional output of the SCN is thus critical for this fundamental biological adaptation to night and day (Panda et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2014b; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: An early microarray study of the SCN identified 650 genes displaying circadian oscillations.
source: An early microarray study of the SCN identified 650 genes displaying circadian oscillations (Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Panda et al. 2002 study.

claim: The number of cycling genes identified in previous studies was limited by the number of genes surveyed, the low signal-to-noise ratio of certain genes, and the use of experimental samples likely to include a large proportion of the surrounding hypothalamic tissue.
source: However, this number will have been limited by the number of genes surveyed, the low signal-to-noise ratio of certain genes (e.g. Per2), and the use of experimental samples likely to include a large proportion of the surrounding hypothalamic tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on methodological limitations of previous studies.

claim: The study of heterogeneous samples will result in reduced amplitudes of oscillations for genes that cycle asynchronously in different brain regions.
source: The study of such heterogeneous samples will result in reduced amplitudes of oscillations for genes that cycle asynchronously in different brain regions (Zhang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al. 2014b.

claim: Over half of all protein-coding genes show circadian oscillations in the mouse.
source: A recent study estimated that over half of all protein-coding genes show circadian oscillations in the mouse, although only 642 could be identified in hypothalamic samples (Zhang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al. 2014b.

claim: Only 642 cycling genes could be identified in hypothalamic samples.
source: A recent study estimated that over half of all protein-coding genes show circadian oscillations in the mouse, although only 642 could be identified in hypothalamic samples (Zhang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al. 2014b.

claim: Many circadian transcriptomic surveys of mammalian systems have utilised constant lighting conditions to focus on the endogenous, free-running circadian clock.
source: Furthermore, many circadian transcriptomic surveys of mammalian systems have utilised constant lighting conditions to focus on the endogenous, free-running circadian clock and have not assessed more physiologically relevant light/dark (LD) cycles (Zhang et al., 2014b; Panda et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 2009; Hurley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous circadian transcriptomic surveys have not assessed more physiologically relevant light/dark (LD) cycles.
source: Furthermore, many circadian transcriptomic surveys of mammalian systems have utilised constant lighting conditions to focus on the endogenous, free-running circadian clock and have not assessed more physiologically relevant light/dark (LD) cycles (Zhang et al., 2014b; Panda et al., 2002; Hughes et al., 2009; Hurley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: LCM accurately isolated the entire SCN for transcriptional profiling.
source: LCM accurately isolated the entire SCN for transcriptional profiling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the figure showing before and after LCM images.

claim: Pooled dissected tissue from five adult male mice provided one of three replicates for each of six timepoints over a 12:12 LD cycle (ZT2, 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22).
source: Pooled dissected tissue from five adult male mice provided one of three replicates for each of six timepoints over a 12:12 LD cycle (ZT2, 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sampling strategy.

claim: Sequencing RNA in each replicate generated up to 133 million paired-end reads of which 45–65% were subsequently mapped to the mouse genome.
source: Sequencing RNA in each replicate generated up to 133 million paired-end reads of which 45–65% were subsequently mapped to the mouse genome allowing for gene expression level estimation.
evidence: This describes the sequencing results and mapping efficiency.

claim: The majority (8/10) of key clock genes show significant cycling (DESeq2 and JTK Cycle; q < 0.05).
source: The majority (8/10) show significant cycling (DESeq2 and JTK Cycle; *q < 0.05) and peak at the expected timepoint denoted by a yellow box (Ko and Takahashi, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap in Figure 1A and statistical analysis.

claim: Key clock genes peak at the expected timepoint.
source: The majority (8/10) show significant cycling (DESeq2 and JTK Cycle; *q < 0.05) and peak at the expected timepoint denoted by a yellow box (Ko and Takahashi, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap in Figure 1A and citation to Ko and Takahashi 2006.

claim: Global expression differences were apparent between timepoints, as revealed by principal component analysis (PCA).
source: Global expression differences were apparent between timepoints, as revealed by principal component analysis (PCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA plot showing separation by timepoint.

claim: Sequencing batch effects are minimal.
source: this verifies the temporal expression of our LCM SCN transcriptome dataset and indicates that any sequencing batch effects are minimal.
evidence: This is inferred from the expected cycling patterns of clock genes.

claim: Quantitative (q)PCR of the LCM SCN samples showed a high degree of concordance with the RNA-seq expression data.
source: Furthermore, quantitative (q)PCR of the LCM SCN samples showed a high degree of concordance with the RNA-seq expression data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis between qPCR and RNA-seq data.

claim: SCN transcriptomes are separable from those in other brain regions and non-CNS tissues.
source: Our SCN transcriptomes are also separable from those in other brain regions and non-CNS tissues (Zhang et al., 2014b; Brawand et al., 2011; Merkin et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012; Barbosa-Morais et al., 2012; Azzi et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis comparing multiple datasets.

claim: Four key SCN markers (Avp, Vip, Grp and Six6) showed a far greater expression enrichment in the SCN over other brain regions.
source: In addition, four key SCN markers (Avp, Vip, Grp and Six6) showed a far greater expression enrichment in the SCN over other brain regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the fold-change enrichment analysis shown in the figure.

claim: 146 genes were identified whose expression is highly enriched in the SCN.
source: A total of 146 genes were identified whose expression is highly enriched in the SCN (Materials and methods; analysis of variance (ANOVA), q < 0.05)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of expression data across tissues.

claim: 4 out of 4 SCN enriched genes were confirmed using in situ hybridisation (ISH).
source: A total of 146 genes were identified whose expression is highly enriched in the SCN (Materials and methods; analysis of variance (ANOVA), q < 0.05) of which 4 out of 4 were confirmed using in situ hybridisation (ISH) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ISH images showing SCN-specific expression.

claim: SCN enriched genes included many known SCN markers, as well as others not previously implicated in circadian biology or in SCN function.
source: These genes included many known SCN markers, as well as others not previously implicated in circadian biology or in SCN function (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with known SCN markers and literature.

claim: SCN enriched genes show significant enrichment for the Mouse Phenotype term 'abnormal circadian rhythm' (q = 1.2×10-4).
source: Their significant enrichments for the Mouse Phenotype term 'abnormal circadian rhythm' (q = 1.2×10-4)
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis using the MGI database.

claim: SCN enriched genes show significant enrichment for Gene Ontology (GO) annotations relating to signalling pathways (q < 0.05).
source: and for Gene Ontology (GO) annotations relating to signalling pathways (q < 0.05; Figure 1B) are consistent with the SCN's role as the master pacemaker.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Enrichment for the flagellum annotation and G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling pathways may reflect the roles of primary cilia as GPCR signalling hubs.
source: Enrichment for the flagellum annotation and G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling pathways (Figure 1B) may reflect the roles of primary cilia as GPCR signalling hubs (Omori et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on enrichment analysis and citation to Omori et al. 2015.

claim: GPCR-mediated neuropeptide signalling via cilia may be important for SCN function.
source: These results thus suggest that GPCR-mediated neuropeptide signalling via cilia may be important for SCN function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the enrichment analysis results.

claim: 4569 genes (24% of 18,889 Ensembl-annotated coding or non-coding models expressed in over six samples) oscillated in a sinusoidal manner.
source: We next identified 4569 genes (24% of 18,889 Ensembl-annotated coding or non-coding models expressed (≥1 read) in over six samples) whose expression oscillated in a sinusoidal manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) according to both JTK Cycle and DESeq2 approaches (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis using JTK Cycle and DESeq2.

claim: The number of cycling genes is sevenfold higher than previously reported in the SCN.
source: Importantly, this number of cycling genes is sevenfold higher than previously reported in the SCN (Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a comparison with the Panda et al. 2002 study.

claim: The large increase in cycling genes is likely to reflect improved anatomical enrichment of the SCN tissue, greater sensitivity and specificity of statistical approaches, and sampling under LD as opposed to DD conditions.
source: This large increase is likely to reflect a combination of factors: first, the significantly improved anatomical enrichment of the SCN tissue we have surveyed; second, the greater sensitivity and specificity of the statistical approaches we have applied (Hughes et al., 2010); and finally, our sampling approach under LD as opposed to the constant dark (DD) conditions utilised in earlier studies (Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on methodological improvements over previous studies.

claim: The sampling approach under LD allows detection of cycling genes that may be physiologically relevant to light exposure or light-induced transcriptional cascades that are undetectable as cycling under DD.
source: For example, we are able to detect cycling genes that may be physiologically relevant to light exposure or light-induced transcriptional cascades that are undetectable as cycling under DD (Ueda et al., 2002; Leming et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing LD-specific cycling genes.

claim: SCN cycling genes were enriched for GO terms relating to key processes such as translation and mitochondrion-related genes.
source: Our new collection of SCN cycling genes were enriched for GO terms relating to key processes such as translation and mitochondrion-related genes, in line with previous findings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; Panda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis and citation to Panda et al. 2002.

claim: De novo transcription has been shown to drive rhythmicity of approximately 20–30% of all cycling genes.
source: De novo transcription has been shown to drive rhythmicity of approximately 20–30% of all cycling genes (Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012), which illustrates the importance of post-transcriptional regulation in shaping the circadian transcriptome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koike et al. 2012 and Menet et al. 2012.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation is important in shaping the circadian transcriptome.
source: De novo transcription has been shown to drive rhythmicity of approximately 20–30% of all cycling genes (Koike et al., 2012; Menet et al., 2012), which illustrates the importance of post-transcriptional regulation in shaping the circadian transcriptome.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that only 20-30% of cycling is driven by de novo transcription.

claim: Novel enrichments among cycling genes in terms relating to RNA splicing and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes suggest that these processes may establish oscillatory expression patterns.
source: Interestingly, we observe novel enrichments among cycling genes in terms relating to RNA splicing and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) which suggests that these processes may establish oscillatory expression patterns (Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on enrichment analysis and citation to Wang et al. 2013.

claim: Approximately half of the SCN cycling genes (2451/4569) showed no evidence for sinusoidal expression in 12 other tissues, including the whole hypothalamus.
source: Approximately half of the SCN cycling genes (2451/4569) showed no evidence for sinusoidal expression in 12 other tissues, including the whole hypothalamus, based on published circadian expression data (JTK Cycle; q < 0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Zhang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published datasets from Zhang et al. 2014b.

claim: Many genes cycle exclusively in the SCN, or only cycle under a 12:12 LD lighting schedule rather than under constant dark conditions.
source: This indicates that many genes cycle exclusively in the SCN, or only cycle under a 12:12 LD lighting schedule rather than under the constant dark conditions used previously (Zhang et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with other tissues and lighting conditions.

claim: Six of the nine genes which cycled significantly across all 12 other tissues also cycled in the LCM SCN samples (Arntl, Dbp, Nr1d2, Per2, Per3 and Tsc22d3).
source: Six of the nine genes which cycled significantly across all 12 other tissues (q < 0.05) also cycled in the LCM SCN samples (Arntl, Dbp, Nr1d2, Per2, Per3 and Tsc22d3) suggesting a core set of universally cycling genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison across multiple tissue datasets.

claim: There is a core set of universally cycling genes.
source: Six of the nine genes which cycled significantly across all 12 other tissues (q < 0.05) also cycled in the LCM SCN samples (Arntl, Dbp, Nr1d2, Per2, Per3 and Tsc22d3) suggesting a core set of universally cycling genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the overlap of cycling genes across tissues.

claim: The LCM SCN cycling gene list significantly overlapped with those cycling in 8 of 12 other tissues (q < 0.05).
source: In support of this notion our LCM SCN cycling gene list significantly overlapped with those cycling in 8 of 12 other tissues (q < 0.05), as well as those cycling in an SCN microarray study (Zhang et al., 2014b; Panda et al., 2002) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of cycling gene lists.

claim: The SCN, hypothalamus and cerebellum showed the greatest overlap of their circadian transcriptomes.
source: As expected, the SCN, hypothalamus and cerebellum showed the greatest overlap of their circadian transcriptomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analysis shown in the figure.

claim: A single module of 766 genes displayed two peaks of expression at ZT14 and ZT22.
source: Using Weighted Correlation Network Analysis (WGCNA), which does not assume a single mode of temporal variation, we identified a single module of 766 genes, which instead of adopting a sinusoidal profile, displayed two peaks of expression at ZT14 and ZT22 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by WGCNA analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: 496 genes from the twin-peaking module individually exhibited statistically significant temporal fluctuations (DESeq2, q < 0.05).
source: From this 'twin-peaking' module 496 genes individually exhibited statistically significant temporal fluctuations (DESeq2, q < 0.05), of which 17 of 17 were validated by qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and qPCR validation.

claim: 17 of 17 twin-peaking genes were validated by qPCR.
source: From this 'twin-peaking' module 496 genes individually exhibited statistically significant temporal fluctuations (DESeq2, q < 0.05), of which 17 of 17 were validated by qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR validation data.

claim: The twin-peaking profile is distinct from previously described 12-hr harmonics.
source: This profile is also distinct from previously described 12-hr harmonics (Cagampang et al., 1998a; 1998b; Hughes et al., 2009), and prior to this, only single genes from individual studies were shown to possess similar expression patterns (Shinohara et al., 1993; Cagampang et al., 1998c; 1998d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on 12-hr harmonics.

claim: Prior to this study, only single genes from individual studies were shown to possess twin-peaking expression patterns.
source: This profile is also distinct from previously described 12-hr harmonics (Cagampang et al., 1998a; 1998b; Hughes et al., 2009), and prior to this, only single genes from individual studies were shown to possess similar expression patterns (Shinohara et al., 1993; Cagampang et al., 1998c; 1998d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Isoforms of protein kinase C (Prkcb and Prkcg) exhibit a twin-peaking profile in rat SCN.
source: For example, isoforms of protein kinase C (Prkcb and Prkcg) exhibit a twin-peaking profile in rat SCN similar to that observed in our RNA-seq data (Cagampang et al., 1998c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cagampang et al. 1998c.

claim: Functional annotations related to synaptic transmission, calcium signalling and gated channel activity were greatly and significantly enriched among twin-peaking genes (q < 0.05).
source: Functional annotations related to synaptic transmission, calcium signalling and gated channel activity were greatly and significantly enriched among these twin-peaking genes (q < 0.05; Figure 2B), suggesting a circadian component to establishing the electrophysiological environment of the SCN.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Twin-peaking genes suggest a circadian component to establishing the electrophysiological environment of the SCN.
source: Functional annotations related to synaptic transmission, calcium signalling and gated channel activity were greatly and significantly enriched among these twin-peaking genes (q < 0.05; Figure 2B), suggesting a circadian component to establishing the electrophysiological environment of the SCN.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the functional enrichment of twin-peaking genes.

claim: The peaking of expression at ZT14 and ZT22 coincides with phase shifting 'susceptibility windows'.
source: The peaking of expression at ZT14 and ZT22 coincides with phase shifting 'susceptibility windows'; time periods in which the photic input permits phase shifting (or 'resetting') of the clock (Ding et al., 1994; Iyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on phase shifting.

claim: A light impulse at ZT14 will initiate a phase delay of the clock.
source: This is demonstrated by the phase response curve (PRC): a light impulse at ZT14 will initiate a phase delay of the clock whereas a light impulse at ZT22 will initiate a phase advance (Figure 2C) (Golombek and Rosenstein, 2010; Ding et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on phase response curves.

claim: A light impulse at ZT22 will initiate a phase advance.
source: This is demonstrated by the phase response curve (PRC): a light impulse at ZT14 will initiate a phase delay of the clock whereas a light impulse at ZT22 will initiate a phase advance (Figure 2C) (Golombek and Rosenstein, 2010; Ding et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on phase response curves.

claim: At all other timepoints assessed under an LD cycle the twin-peaking genes exhibited low expression levels exactly when the clock is resistant to phase shifts.
source: At all other timepoints we assessed under an LD cycle the twin-peaking genes exhibited low expression levels exactly when the clock is resistant to phase shifts.
evidence: This is supported by the expression data and comparison with the phase response curve.

claim: A threshold level of gene expression needs to be exceeded for light to activate the phase shifting pathway.
source: This suggests a possible transcriptional gating mechanism in which a threshold level of gene expression needs to be exceeded for light to activate this phase shifting pathway (Ding et al., 1994; Gillette and Mitchell, 2002; Iyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between expression and phase shifting susceptibility.

claim: Genes previously known to participate in the light-induced phase shifting pathway display the twin-peaking pattern.
source: Genes previously known to participate in this light-induced phase shifting pathway display this twin-peaking pattern (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by the pathway diagram in Figure 2D showing twin-peaking genes.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Grin2a/b, Camk2a, Nos1, and Ryr2 blocks light-induced phase shifts.
source: and their pharmacological inhibition (e.g. for Grin2a/b, Camk2a, Nos1, Ryr2) blocks light-induced phase shifts (Ebling et al., 1991; Yokota et al., 2001; Ding et al., 1998; 1994; 2007; 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: Many genes whose expression peaks singly at ZT14 have functions related to actin cytoskeleton reorganisation and/or to small GTPase signalling.
source: Many genes whose expression peaks singly at ZT14 have functions related to actin cytoskeleton reorganisation and/or to small GTPase signalling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis and peak phase distribution.

claim: Actin depolymerisation is important for phase delays but not phase advances.
source: This supports the hypothesis that actin depolymerisation is important for phase delays but not phase advances (Gerber et al., 2013; Cabej, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on actin and phase shifting.

claim: Oscillations in the SCN transcriptome play an important role in gating the differential responses to light.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that oscillations in the SCN transcriptome play an important role in gating the differential responses to light, a fundamental circadian process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the twin-peaking gene analysis and their correlation with phase shifting.

claim: Light exposure during constant conditions can modify the processing of non-photic signals by the SCN.
source: Light exposure during constant conditions can still modify the processing of non-photic signals by the SCN (Challet and Pevet, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Challet and Pevet 2003.

claim: Novelty-induced running in the subjective mid-day induces a phase advance in mice.
source: For example, novelty-induced running in the subjective mid-day induces a phase advance in mice, although a 1-hr light pulse administered after access to running wheels can significantly attenuate this affect (Biello and Mrosovsky, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Biello and Mrosovsky 1995.

claim: A 1-hr light pulse administered after access to running wheels can significantly attenuate the phase advance induced by novelty-induced running.
source: For example, novelty-induced running in the subjective mid-day induces a phase advance in mice, although a 1-hr light pulse administered after access to running wheels can significantly attenuate this affect (Biello and Mrosovsky, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Biello and Mrosovsky 1995.

claim: 3187 multiexonic long intergenic non-coding RNA (lincRNAs; >200 nucleotides) loci were identified from the SCN transcriptome data.
source: A total of 3187 multiexonic long intergenic non-coding RNA (lincRNAs; >200 nucleotides) loci were identified from the SCN transcriptome data.
evidence: This is supported by the lincRNA identification pipeline applied to the RNA-seq data.

claim: Identified lincRNAs displayed evidence of significant sequence conservation.
source: Considered together, they displayed evidence of significant sequence conservation, had lower expression and fewer exons than protein-coding genes in line with lncRNAs identified in other mammalian tissues (Zhang et al., 2014a; Cabili et al., 2011; Ponjavic et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Identified lincRNAs had lower expression than protein-coding genes.
source: Considered together, they displayed evidence of significant sequence conservation, had lower expression and fewer exons than protein-coding genes in line with lncRNAs identified in other mammalian tissues (Zhang et al., 2014a; Cabili et al., 2011; Ponjavic et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by expression comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Identified lincRNAs had fewer exons than protein-coding genes.
source: Considered together, they displayed evidence of significant sequence conservation, had lower expression and fewer exons than protein-coding genes in line with lncRNAs identified in other mammalian tissues (Zhang et al., 2014a; Cabili et al., 2011; Ponjavic et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by exon number comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Identified lincRNAs did not display correlated expression with that of the nearest protein-coding gene suggesting these lincRNAs are often not functioning as enhancer (e)RNAs.
source: but did not display correlated expression with that of the nearest protein-coding gene suggesting these lincRNAs are often not functioning as enhancer (e)RNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 341 (11%) of the identified lincRNAs displayed significant temporal fluctuation.
source: Of these lincRNAs, 341 (11%) displayed significant temporal fluctuation
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of lincRNA expression over time.

claim: The presence of lincRNA NONCO7761 (3100003L05Rik) in the SCN was confirmed by ISH at ZT6.
source: including lincRNA NONCO7761 (3100003L05Rik) whose presence in the SCN was confirmed by ISH at ZT6 (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by ISH image in Figure 3D.

claim: lincRNA NONCO7761 (3100003L05Rik) peaks at both ZT6 and ZT18 as confirmed by qPCR.
source: as well as by qPCR to peak at both ZT6 and ZT18 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 3E.

claim: 28 fluctuating lincRNAs peaked at ZT14 and ZT22.
source: In addition, 28 of these fluctuating lincRNAs peaked at ZT14 and ZT22 (Figure 3B–C)
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap in Figure 3C showing twin-peaking lincRNAs.

claim: Twin-peaking lincRNAs may modulate or be modulated by the transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulation of protein-coding genes of the twin-peaking synaptic module.
source: and thus may modulate or be modulated by the transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulation of protein-coding genes of the twin-peaking synaptic module described earlier.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the temporal correlation between twin-peaking lincRNAs and protein-coding genes.

claim: 1013 novel exons were identified – transcribed regions of the transcriptome which have not been annotated by Ensembl or UCSC, but contribute to alternative transcripts in a known gene.
source: We also identified 1013 novel exons – transcribed regions of the transcriptome which have not been annotated by Ensembl or UCSC, but contribute to alternative transcripts in a known gene.
evidence: This is supported by de novo transcript assembly and filtering criteria.

claim: A novel exon of the core clock gene Cry1 appears to represent an alternative transcriptional start site (TSS).
source: Of these, we focused on the novel exon of the core clock gene Cry1 which appears to represent an alternative transcriptional start site (TSS) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the genomic structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The novel exon of Cry1 is 322 bp in size.
source: Despite its large size (322 bp) and high expression, the novel exon present in the first intron of Cry1 had remained elusive, yet is confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from SCN tissue (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the novel Cry1 exon.

claim: The novel exon of Cry1 is highly expressed.
source: Despite its large size (322 bp) and high expression, the novel exon present in the first intron of Cry1 had remained elusive, yet is confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from SCN tissue (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the novel Cry1 exon.

claim: The novel exon of Cry1 is present in the first intron of Cry1.
source: Despite its large size (322 bp) and high expression, the novel exon present in the first intron of Cry1 had remained elusive, yet is confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from SCN tissue (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The novel exon of Cry1 is confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from SCN tissue.
source: Despite its large size (322 bp) and high expression, the novel exon present in the first intron of Cry1 had remained elusive, yet is confirmed by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from SCN tissue (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The novel and canonical Cry1 isoforms are expressed in antiphase.
source: The novel and canonical Cry1 isoforms are expressed in antiphase, as confirmed by qPCR from LCM SCN samples (Figure 4D), indicating an unanticipated mode of temporal regulation in the SCN for this core clock gene.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The antiphase expression of Cry1 isoforms indicates an unanticipated mode of temporal regulation in the SCN for this core clock gene.
